s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Fear, Terror, Alarm
s.d: a state of severe distress, aroused by intense concern for impending pain, danger, evil, etc., or possibly by the illusion of such circumstances
s.c: In a number of languages there is no noun-like word for ‘fear.’ Accordingly, expressions containing such a noun in Greek must often be restructured so that the corresponding semantic unit may be expressed by a verb. Therefore, instead of ‘fear,’ one may have expressions such as ‘be afraid’ or ‘to fear.’ Instead of ‘fears within’ (⟦2 Corinthians 7:5|2 Corinthians 7:5⟧), one may translate ‘in our hearts we were afraid.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Fear, Terror, Alarm
s.d: the occasion or source of fear
s.c: φόβος in the sense of ‘source of fear’ is essentially a causative, so that ⟦Romans 13:3|Romans 13:3⟧ may often be rendered as ‘for the rulers do not cause those who do good to fear but cause those who do what is bad to fear.’

s.d: branch of the palm tree (φοῖνιξ{N:001})
s.c: βάϊον is a technical term meaning ‘palm branch,’ and in ⟦John 12:13|John 12:13⟧ τῶν φοινίκων ‘of palm trees’ may have been added redundantly, since the term βάϊον may not have been regarded as sufficiently well known to readers.|In the contexts in which φοῖνιξ (⟦John 12:13|John 12:13⟧; see LN 3.8) and φοῖνιξ (⟦Revelation 7:9|Revelation 7:9⟧) occur in the NT, it is important to obtain a satisfactory term for branch, since in a number of languages a very important distinction is made between branches of palm trees, which are often called leaves (technically they are), and branches of most other trees (often spoken of idiomatically as arms of the trees).

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Punishment and Execution
s.d: an instrument consisting of either a single or multiple strips of leather with or without weighted tips on the ends; used to strike animals to make them move (faster), or as punishment on humans
s.c: The weighted tips of a φραγέλλιον would normally have been made of metal so as to increase the force of the blow and to inflict more severe punishment.

s.d: to beat severely with a whip
s.g: to whip; to beat with a whip; whipping; flogging

s.d: a structure for enclosing an open area
s.c: In practically all societies there is some type of fence, wall, or barrier employed to surround fields. In some instances this may consist of piled up logs or sticks; in other instances the wall may be made of packed dirt or of laid-up stone. What is important, however, is not the form, but the function, and therefore one may often use a descriptive expression, for example, ‘a barrier to surround a field,’ sometimes described as ‘a barrier to keep animals out of the field.’|φραγμός is also used figuratively of the Law, which constituted a barrier between Jews and Gentiles: τὸ μεσότοιχον τοῦ φραγμοῦ ‘a wall of separation’ or ‘barrier’ ⟦Ephesians 2:14|Ephesians 2:14⟧. In ⟦Ephesians 2:14|Ephesians 2:14⟧ φραγμός may be rendered as ‘a wall to keep apart’ or ‘a wall to divide’ (see LN 34.39).

s.d: a path or area along a fence, wall, or hedge (where desperately poor people might stay)

s.dp: Association › Belong To, Be Included in the Membership of, Be Excluded From
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:φραγμός<SDBG:φραγμός:000000>}[a] ‘fence,’ {D:7.59}) that which serves as a means of separation in interpersonal relations
s.g: that which separates; that which isolates
s.c: In a number of languages, however, it may be necessary to indicate what or who is separated, and therefore one may need to translate this phrase in ⟦Ephesians 2:14|Ephesians 2:14⟧ as ‘… that separates Jews from Gentiles.’

s.d: to explain the meaning of something, with the implication that the text in question is difficult or complex
to cause something to cease (used with special reference to speech)
s.g: to cause to cease; to stop

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to block the mouth) to cause someone not to have anything to say
s.g: to silence; to remove any reason to speak

s.dp: Violence, Harm, Destroy, Kill › Harm, Wound
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to shut the mouth) to prevent harm or injury being done (in the one context in the NT, {S:05801103300020}, a reference to lions)
s.g: to stop the mouth of; to keep from harming
s.c: The particular historical reference of this phrase in ⟦Hebrews 11:33|Hebrews 11:33⟧ is not clear. In the account in ⟦Daniel 6:22|Daniel 6:22⟧ it is the angel of God which shut the mouths of the lions.

s.d: deep constructions, often walled with stone, at the bottom of which was a pool of water
s.c: If there was a relatively ready flow of water, a well could very appropriately be called a πηγή ‘spring,’ LN 1.78 (and this may be the reason for πηγή in ⟦John 4:6|John 4:6⟧), but if water only gradually seeped into the well from surrounding areas or was collected in the well from surface drainage, it would be more appropriately called φρέαρ. However, both terms are used interchangeably in certain contexts; compare, for example, πηγή in ⟦John 4:6|John 4:6⟧ and φρέαρ in ⟦John 4:11|John 4:11⟧, both referring to Jacob’s well at Sychar.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Depressions and Holes
s.d: a relatively deep pit or shaft in the ground
s.c: In this occurrence of φρέαρ (⟦Revelation 9:1|Revelation 9:1⟧), the reference is essentially equivalent to that of ἄβυσσος ‘abyss’ (LN 1.20).

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Hold a Wrong View, Be Mistaken

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Hold a Wrong View, Be Mistaken
s.d: (derivative of {L:φρεναπατάω<SDBG:φρεναπατάω:000000>} ‘to lead astray,’ {D:31.12}) one who misleads people concerning the truth
s.c: In some languages the equivalent of φρεναπάτης is ‘one who leads along the wrong path’ or ‘one who says wrong is right.’

s.d: the psychological faculty of thoughtful planning, often with the implication of being wise and provident
s.g: thoughtful planning; way of thinking; outlook

s.g: to shudder with fear; to be extremely afraid

s.d: (derivative of the base φρον ‘thoughtful planning,’ {D:26.15}) to employ one’s faculty for thoughtful planning, with emphasis upon the underlying disposition or attitude
s.g: to have an attitude; to think in a particular manner
s.c: In some instances it may be appropriate to render ⟦Philippians 2:5|Philippians 2:5⟧ as ‘you should think the way Christ Jesus did’ or ‘how Jesus Christ thought about things is the way you should think about them’ (in which a term meaning ‘things’ would refer to events and not simply to material objects).|It is also possible to understand φρονέω in ⟦Philippians 2:5|Philippians 2:5⟧ as referring specifically to the attitude of people to one another.

s.d: to keep on giving serious consideration to something
s.g: to ponder; to let one’s mind dwell on; to keep thinking about; to fix one’s attention on

s.dp: Hold a View, Believe, Trust › Have an Opinion, Hold a View
s.d: to hold a view or have an opinion with regard to something

s.d: the psychological faculty of thoughtful planning, often with the implication of being wise and provident
s.g: thoughtful planning; way of thinking; outlook

s.d: the ability to understand, as the result of insight and wisdom
s.g: capacity to understand; wisdom; being wise

s.d: pertaining to understanding resulting from insight and wisdom
s.g: wise; wisely; with understanding; with insight

s.d: pertaining to understanding resulting from insight and wisdom
s.g: wise; wisely; with understanding; with insight

s.d: to keep on giving serious consideration to something
s.g: to ponder; to let one’s mind dwell on; to keep thinking about; to fix one’s attention on

s.d: to be on one’s guard against some eventuality
s.g: to guard against; to keep under watch; to watch over
s.c: In a number of languages there is a great deal of difference in terminology employed in speaking about guarding an area in order to apprehend someone and guarding a flock of animals for fear of theft from robbers or danger from wild animals.

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Anger, Be Indignant With
s.d: to show insolent anger
s.c: φρυάσσω evidently combines not only anger but a considerable measure of opposition, both verbal and nonverbal.

s.d: dry branches of trees or shrubs broken or cut into suitable lengths for use as firewood

s.d: a Christian in Asia who with Hermogenes turned his back on Paul

s.dp: Linear Movement › Leave, Depart, Flee, Escape, Send
s.d: to move quickly from a point or area in order to avoid presumed danger or difficulty
s.g: to run away; to flee; flight

s.d: a place of detention
s.c: Practically all languages have terms for a jail or a prison, though in some instances a descriptive phrase is employed, ‘a place where people are tied up’ or ‘a place to be chained.’ In some instances, highly idiomatic expressions are used, ‘a place for eating iron’ or ‘a room with rats.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:φυλάσσω<SDBG:φυλάσσω:000000>}[a] ‘to guard closely,’ {D:37.120}) a place or post for guarding

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: one of four periods of time into which the night was divided (during which time certain assigned persons would be on the lookout)
s.g: watch; a fourth of the night
s.c: In general, φυλακή in the NT refers to one of four periods into which the night was divided, based on the Roman custom of dividing the night into four equal periods or watches. In ⟦Matthew 24:43|Matthew 24:43⟧ and ⟦Luke 12:38|Luke 12:38⟧, however, it is possible that the reference is to three night watches, as was typical among Hebrews and Greeks.

s.d: a place for wild animals and evil spirits to dwell
to be on one’s guard against some eventuality
s.g: to guard against; to keep under watch; to watch over
s.c: In a number of languages there is a great deal of difference in terminology employed in speaking about guarding an area in order to apprehend someone and guarding a flock of animals for fear of theft from robbers or danger from wild animals.

s.d: to confine someone in prison
s.g: to imprison; imprisonment; to put in jail
s.c: ‘To imprison a person’ is often expressed in somewhat idiomatic forms, for example, ‘to be tied inside’ or ‘to be locked in the dark’ or even ‘to eat one’s food with rats.’

s.d: a small leather case containing OT scripture verses and worn on the arm and forehead by Jews, especially when praying
s.c: The Greek word φυλακτήριον, both before and during NT times, referred to an object used as a means of protection from evil forces. As such, it constituted a kind of amulet, but in ⟦Matthew 23:5|Matthew 23:5⟧ φυλακτήριον is a reference to what was called in Aramaic tephillin, meaning ‘prayers.’ The two phylacteries, one worn on the head and the other on the left arm, were bound on during daily morning prayers. Just what their function seems to have been is not certain. In ⟦Matthew 23:5|Matthew 23:5⟧, Jesus does not condemn the use of such phylacteries, but he does denounce their ostentatious use.

s.d: one who is responsible for guarding an area or a person
to hold someone or something in close custody
to continue to obey orders or commandments
s.g: to obey; to keep commandments; obedience

s.d: to make a distinct effort to keep oneself from doing something
s.g: to be careful not to; to make an effort not to; to seriously avoid; to keep from

s.d: to be on one’s guard against some eventuality
s.g: to guard against; to keep under watch; to watch over
s.c: In a number of languages there is a great deal of difference in terminology employed in speaking about guarding an area in order to apprehend someone and guarding a flock of animals for fear of theft from robbers or danger from wild animals.

s.dp: Kinship Terms › Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
s.d: a subgroup of a nation which is regarded as being more closely related biologically than the entire nation
s.c: In a number of societies there are only three well-defined biologically related groups: (1) the nuclear family (that is to say, the immediate family); (2) the extended family (often referred to as ‘the clan’); and (3) the tribe or nation as a whole. Under such circumstances it may be necessary to speak of the twelve tribes of Israel as being ‘twelve large clans.’ This would emphasize their biological relationships and at the same time would suggest that they constituted part of a larger ethnic unit, namely, the nation. On the other hand, a number of so-called ‘primitive societies’ have a great many designations for different sets of biologically related persons. These may designate an individual family, an extended family, the clan, a grouping of clans, a division of a tribe into two interacting units (called moieties), and finally the tribe as a whole, equivalent in larger societies to a nation. The choice of appropriate terms for various groups of biologically related persons becomes particularly complex in certain passages in the OT.

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Political
s.d: a relatively large unit of people who constitute a sociopolitical group, sharing a presumed biological descent (in many contexts {L:πατριά<SDBG:πατριά:000001>}[b] and φυλή[b] are very similar in meaning to {L:ἔθνος<SDBG:ἔθνος:000000>}[a], {D:11.55}){N:001}

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: (a set phrase, literally: the twelve tribes, but used in a figurative sense) all of the people of God as a possible reference to the new Israel
s.c: It is possible to understand ⟦James 1:1|James 1:1⟧ as containing a salutation to the twelve tribes of Israel scattered throughout the Diaspora, but this literal interpretation has generally been rejected for a reference to all of God’s people scattered throughout the known world. If one elects to follow a literal translation of this passage, it would be important to introduce a marginal note indicating the alternative meaning and vice versa.

Some languages make a clear distinction between various kinds of leaves, especially a difference between leaves which have parallel veins and those which have branching veins. In ⟦Mark 11:13|Mark 11:13⟧ what is important is that the fig tree was ‘in leaf,’ that is to say, the leaves had already come out after the winter season. In a number of languages a tree in this state may be referred to as ‘a tree which is green.’

s.dp: Features of Objects › Two-Dimensional and Three-Dimensional Shapes
s.d: a three-dimensional object with irregular rounding contours
(derivative of φυράω ‘to mix substances’ such as flour, either with other dry substances or with water, not occurring in the NT) that which is mixed or kneaded
pertaining to that which is in accordance with the nature or character of something
s.g: natural; naturally; by nature; by instinct
s.c: For some languages the equivalent of ‘being in accordance with nature’ is simply ‘being as it should be’ (⟦Romans 1:26|Romans 1:26⟧). For ⟦2 Peter 2:12|2 Peter 2:12⟧, in place of an expression such as ‘natural creatures’ a more appropriate equivalent in some languages is simply ‘animals.’

s.d: pertaining to that which is in accordance with the nature or character of something
s.g: natural; naturally; by nature; by instinct

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Arrogance, Haughtiness, Pride
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of φυσιόω ‘to puff up, to inflate,’ not occurring in the NT) to cause someone to be proud, arrogant, or haughty
s.g: to make proud; to make arrogant; to make haughty

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Arrogance, Haughtiness, Pride
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of φυσιόω ‘to puff up, to inflate,’ not occurring in the NT) to be puffed up with pride
s.g: to be proud; to be haughty

s.d: the nature of something as the result of its natural development or condition
s.c: For languages in which there is no ready equivalent to the lexical term ‘nature,’ it may be possible to render the expression in ⟦Galatians 4:8|Galatians 4:8⟧ as ‘beings who are really not gods,’ and in ⟦2 Peter 1:4|2 Peter 1:4⟧ one may translate ‘to share in what God is like’ or ‘to be like God in certain ways.’

s.d: a class of entities based on physiological and genetic similarity

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Arrogance, Haughtiness, Pride
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of φυσίωσις ‘inflation,’ not occurring in the NT) an inflated, puffed up, exaggerated view of one’s own importance
any kind of plant, whether tree, bush, or herb
s.c: The principal translational difficulty with φυτεία is that in so many languages there is no term with such a generic meaning. Sometimes the closest equivalent is a descriptive phrase ‘green things’ or ‘leafy things.’|Classifications of plants vary greatly from one language to another. Principal distinctions are based upon size, woodiness, perennials versus annuals, and food-producing in contrast with non-food-producing.

s.d: to plant, used primarily in relation to vines, bushes, and trees

s.dp: Physiological Processes and States › Grow, Growth
s.d: to grow (of plants)
s.c: In ⟦Hebrews 12:15|Hebrews 12:15⟧ φύω occurs in an extended figurative context which may be better treated as a simile. Compare, for example, a literal translation of μή τις ῥίζα πικρίας ἄνω φύουσα ‘lest any root of bitterness grow up’ with the treatment of this expression as a type of simile, ‘in order that no one becomes like a bitter plant that grows up.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Depressions and Holes
s.d: a hole, typically occupied by an animal as a den or lair
s.c: In most languages it is important to make a distinction between φωλεός as in ⟦Luke 9:58|Luke 9:58⟧ and ὀπή ‘hole’ (LN 1.53), for φωλεός is normally some type of hole serving as a typical habitation or place of escape for an animal, while ὀπή in ⟦Hebrews 11:38|Hebrews 11:38⟧ would not be a place of normal habitation.

s.d: to communicate directly or indirectly to someone who is presumably at a distance, in order to tell such a person to come{N:001}
to speak with considerable volume or loudness{N:002}
s.g: to cry out; to shout; to call out; to speak loudly

s.d: to use an attribution in speaking of a person
s.c: It is not always possible to determine from the context whether the act involved is an initial naming of a person or simply calling a person by a particular name. Likewise in the case of attributions or titles, it is not always possible to determine whether it is a matter of giving an attribution or title to a person or simply a matter of speaking of or to a person by means of such an attribution or title. In some instances the giving of a title may be made indirect. For example, in ⟦Matthew 1:23|Matthew 1:23⟧ the statement ‘and they will call his name Emmanuel’ suggests the giving of a title, but the process is stated in terms of how people will speak of this person.

s.d: to ask a person to accept offered hospitality{N:003}
to produce a sound
s.c: Though in ⟦Matthew 26:75|Matthew 26:75⟧ one may wish to use a more specific term such as ‘crows,’ the meaning of φωνέω is simply ‘to produce a sound.’

s.d: any type of sound, including human speech, but normally a distinctive type of sound as opposed to confused noise
s.c: In many languages an important distinction is made between verbal sounds, that is to say, the sounds of speech, and non-verbal sounds. In some languages musical sounds also require a very special type of terminology, often with distinctions made depending upon the type of instrument involved.

s.d: the human voice as an instrument of communication
s.c: In a number of languages one cannot speak of a voice without identifying who is speaking, and since the context indicates clearly that this is God, one can only say ‘God’s voice came from the cloud’ or ‘God spoke from a cloud.’

s.d: the sound of a cry or shout
a verbal code, whether oral or written, as a basic means of communication
s.c: It is possible to interpret φωνή in ⟦2 Peter 2:16|2 Peter 2:16⟧ as ‘voice’ (see LN 33.103).

s.d: light, in contrast with darkness ({L:σκότος<SDBG:σκότος:000000>}[a], {L:σκοτία<SDBG:σκοτία:000000>}[a], {D:14.53}), usually in relationship to some source of light such as the sun, moon, fire, lamp, etc.{N:001}
s.c: Terms for ‘light’ often differ on the basis of whether there is a specific source of light, for example, a fire, lamps, sun, moon, etc., or whether the light is simply generalized, in the sense of daylight apart from the actual shining of the sun (for example, as in the interior of a room). Some languages also make distinctions between terms for light depending on whether the light comes from a fire or lamp or from a heavenly body.|In a number of languages there is no noun for ‘light,’ but only verbs are employed, since the fact of light is spoken of as something which happens and is hence regarded as an event.

s.d: a pile or heap of burning material
s.c: The Greek phrase ἅψαντες … πυράν ‘to kindle a fire’ is best rendered in a number of languages by a single verb meaning ‘to make a fire,’ and in some languages it is strange to speak of a ‘fire’ without indicating the type of material which is being burned. Hence, in ⟦Acts 28:2|Acts 28:2⟧ the appropriate equivalent would be ‘they caused some sticks to burn.’|In some languages a very important distinction is made between two functionally different kinds of fire, one used for getting rid of refuse and the other used for warming oneself. Fire as a destructive agent, mentioned frequently in the book of Revelation (⟦Revelation 8:5|Revelation 8:5⟧ and ⟦Revelation 20:10|Revelation 20:10⟧), may require quite a different term from what is used in speaking of a fire for the purpose of warming a person or heating an object.

s.d: a stick or bundle of sticks carried about as a light
s.c: It is, of course, possible that in ⟦Acts 16:29|Acts 16:29⟧ the meaning of φῶς is a lamp (see LN 6.104).

s.dp: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes › Socio-Religious
s.d: (idioms, literally: sons of the light, and: children of light, respectively) persons to whom the truth of God has been revealed and who are presumably living according to such truth. See also {D:9.4} and {D:12.15}
s.g: sons of the light; children of the light; people of God
s.c: In a number of languages it is difficult to speak of ‘light’ in the metaphorical sense of the truth that comes from God. Such truth is not to be equated with knowledge, but with the principles and practices of right moral behavior. Because of these difficulties in speaking of ‘truth’ as ‘light,’ a number of translators have preferred to use the expression ‘people of God’ for the phrases υἱοὶ τοῦ φωτός, υἱοὶ τῆς ἡμέρας, and τέκνα φωτός. In some instances, however, it is possible to employ ‘light,’ if this is described as ‘light that comes from God’ or even ‘the true light from God.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: in the light) pertaining to being widely known in view of the events in question having taken place in public{N:002}

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Heavenly Bodies
s.d: any light-producing object in the sky, such as the sun, moon, and other planets and stars
s.c: Though φωστήρ may refer to any light-producing object, it is used especially of the heavenly bodies and more specifically of stars, as in ⟦Philippians 2:15|Philippians 2:15⟧, the one NT context in which φωστήρ occurs. A focal component of this meaning is the light-giving characteristic.

s.d: the state of brightness or shining
s.c: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between some object which is bright in and of itself (that is to say, the source of brightness or radiance) and objects which are bright because they reflect light from some source. In the case of ⟦Matthew 17:5|Matthew 17:5⟧ (which is generally regarded as a reference to the Shekinah presence of God), the cloud would not be merely reflecting light but would be a source of light (see LN 14.50).

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Heavenly Bodies
s.d: a light-producing heavenly body, probably the morning star (a planet), but possibly the sun
s.c: The literal meaning of φωσφόρος is ‘that which bears light,’ but it is a conventional reference to the morning star, which in reality is not a star, but one of the brighter planets, usually Venus, but also Jupiter, Mars, Mercury, or even Saturn. In the one occurrence of this word in the NT, namely, ⟦2 Peter 1:19|2 Peter 1:19⟧, φωσφόρος is an indirect figurative reference to Jesus and his redemptive work, but it is extremely difficult in a number of languages to speak of ‘the light of the morning star shining in your hearts.’ One may sometimes say ‘… shines upon your hearts’ or possibly ‘… shines upon you and causes you to have new hearts’ or ‘… and illumines your minds.’

s.d: pertaining to being well lighted
s.c: In a number of languages one cannot speak of an object being ‘full of light,’ for light is not spoken of as a substance. It is, of course, normally possible to speak of something as ‘having light inside’ (for example, the occurrence of light within a room). However, rather than speaking positively of the occurrence of light, it is sometimes more satisfactory to indicate the absence of darkness, for example, ‘there was no darkness there’ or, as in ⟦Matthew 6:22|Matthew 6:22⟧, ‘your whole body will have no darkness in it.’

s.d: pertaining to being bright or shining, either of a source or of an object which is illuminated by a source
to cause light to shine upon some object, in the sense of illuminating it
s.c: Expressions involving the causing of light to shine upon an object often involve explicit causative elements, for example, ‘to cause light to shine upon’ or ‘to cause to shine’ or ‘to cause to be bright’ or ‘to cause to be in the light.’

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: to cause something to be fully known by revealing clearly and in some detail{N:001}
s.g: to make known; to make plain; to reveal; to bring to the light; to disclose; revelation

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of φωτισμός ‘light,’ not occurring in the NT) that which has been revealed as true

s.dp: Know › Well Known, Clearly Shown, Revealed
s.d: to cause something to be fully known by revealing clearly and in some detail{N:001}
s.g: to make known; to make plain; to reveal; to bring to the light; to disclose; revelation

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Happy, Glad, Joyful
s.d: to enjoy a state of happiness and well-being
to employ a formalized expression of greeting, implying a wish for happiness on the part of the person greeted
s.c: The functional equivalent of χαίρω in Spanish would be que viva. In traditional English one might employ an expression such as long live!

s.d: frozen rain
s.c: In ⟦Revelation 8:7|Revelation 8:7⟧ and ⟦Revelation 16:21|Revelation 16:21⟧ it is possible that χάλαζα is better interpreted as referring to a ‘hailstorm.’|In a number of languages hail is described as ‘frozen rain,’ but it may be referred to by more idiomatic expressions such as ‘cloud stones’ or ‘ice stones.’

s.d: to cause something to move down gradually

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of Χαλδαία ‘Chaldea,’ not occurring in the NT) a person who is a native of Chaldea

s.dp: Trouble, Hardship, Relief, Favorable Circumstances › Difficult, Hard
s.d: pertaining to that which causes trouble and hardship, with an implication of violence
s.c: It may be very difficult in some languages to speak of ‘troublous times,’ for ‘trouble’ seems to relate to human experience and not to circumstances. Therefore, this expression in ⟦2 Timothy 3:1|2 Timothy 3:1⟧ can perhaps be best rendered in some languages as ‘in the last days, people will suffer very much.’

s.d: pertaining to one who is inclined to violent and dangerous activity

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Self-Control, Lack of Self-Control
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of χαλιναγωγέω ‘to control with bit or bridle,’ not occurring in the NT) to exercise close control over some function
s.c: In some languages the expression μὴ χαλιναγωγῶν γλῶσσαν αὐτοῦ in ⟦James 1:26|James 1:26⟧ may be rendered as ‘one who does not tell his tongue what to say’ or ‘one who cannot tie his tongue down’ or ‘one who cannot stop his talking.’

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Agriculture and Husbandry
s.d: items used to control the actions of a horse, consisting of a bit (a short metal bar placed in the mouth of a horse) and bridle (ropes or leather straps attached to the bit and fitted over the horse’s head)
s.c: In languages in which a bit or bridle as a piece of harness is not known, one can employ a descriptive phrase, ‘something to guide a horse with’ or ‘something to put in the mouth of a horse to guide it.’|In ⟦Revelation 14:20|Revelation 14:20⟧ the reference to a bit and bridle is merely an indication of measurement, that is to say, the height of the bit and bridle from the ground, and one may reinterpret this measurement as ‘about a meter and a half’ or ‘about five feet.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:χαλκός<SDBG:χαλκός:000000>}[a] ‘bronze, brass, copper,’ {D:2.54}) one who makes objects out of brass, bronze, copper, or other metals

s.dp: Natural Substances › Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
s.d: agate, chalcedony, usually milky or gray in color (see {D:2.29})
a container or object made of copper, brass, or bronze
s.c: In a number of languages the most natural equivalent of χαλκίον is ‘metal vessel’ or ‘kettle.’

s.d: a particularly valuable or fine type of bronze or brass, possibly even an alloy containing some gold
s.c: In the two references with χαλκολίβανον in the NT (⟦Revelation 1:15|Revelation 1:15⟧ and ⟦Revelation 2:18|Revelation 2:18⟧) the emphasis is upon the lustrous appearance of the metal. A satisfactory equivalent may be ‘bright bronze’ or ‘shining metal.’

s.d: generally bronze (an alloy of copper and tin), but in some contexts apparently brass (an alloy of copper and zinc) and perhaps in a few instances copper
s.c: Most archaeological objects of the Middle East containing copper consist of bronze, and therefore the most accurate translation of χαλκός is in most instances a term for bronze, which is harder than brass and much harder than pure copper. Many languages have technical terms for bronze, brass, and copper, but some simply designate bronze as ‘brown metal,’ brass as ‘bright metal,’ and copper as ‘red metal.’

s.d: coins of bronze or copper, and hence of little value{N:001}
(an idiom, literally: echoing brass, or: resounding brass) a gong made of brass
s.c: In a number of languages the equivalent of gong is ‘noisy metal’ or ‘reverberating metal’ or ‘echoing metal,’ but frequently translators have simply used an expression meaning ‘loud bell.’

s.d: (derivative of {L:χαλκός<SDBG:χαλκός:000000>}[a] ‘bronze, brass, copper,’ {D:2.54}) pertaining to being made or consisting of bronze, brass, or copper

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › The Earth's Surface
s.d: a location on the surface of the earth
s.g: on the ground; to the ground

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: the land west of the Jordan river

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: (derivative of {L:Χανάαν<SDBG:Χανάαν:000000>} ‘Canaan,’ {D:93.611}) pertaining to Canaan

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Happy, Glad, Joyful
s.d: a state of joy and gladness
s.c: In a number of languages ‘joy’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘my heart is dancing’ or ‘my heart shouts because I am happy.’

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Happy, Glad, Joyful
s.d: that which is the cause of joy or gladness
s.g: cause of joy; reason for gladness

s.d: a meaningful mark, whether engraved, imprinted, or branded
s.c: A strictly literal translation of ‘the mark of the beast’ might imply ‘a picture of the beast’ or ‘a mark made by the beast.’ A more satisfactory indication of the relationship between ‘mark’ and ‘beast’ would be ‘a mark showing one’s relationship to the beast’ or ‘a mark of loyalty to the beast’ or ‘a mark of the party of the beast.’

s.d: an object (not necessarily three-dimensional) which has been formed to resemble a person, god, animal, etc.
s.c: In certain contexts the referents of εἰκών, τύπος, and χάραγμα may have special religious significance in that they may refer to idols, but the focal component for the translator is that of a likeness or resemblance. In contexts such as ⟦Matthew 22:20|Matthew 22:20⟧ an equivalent translation may be simply ‘a picture,’ but in ⟦Romans 1:23|Romans 1:23⟧ and ⟦Acts 7:43|Acts 7:43⟧ one may use the same expression as is employed to render εἴδωλον ‘idol’ (LN 6.97).

s.dp: Nature, Class, Example › Pattern, Model, Example, and Corresponding Representation
s.d: a representation as an exact reproduction of a particular form or structure
a fence of poles or stakes used to fortify entrenchments
s.c: In ⟦Luke 19:43|Luke 19:43⟧ barricades may be rendered in some instances as ‘thick walls’ or ‘strong fences.’

s.d: to give or grant graciously and generously, with the implication of good will on the part of the giver{N:001}
s.g: to give; to grant; to bestow generously

s.d: to forgive, on the basis of one’s gracious attitude toward an individual
s.c: It may be useful in some instances to translate χαρίζομαι in ⟦2 Corinthians 12:13|2 Corinthians 12:13⟧ as ‘be so kind as to forgive me.’

s.dp: Possess, Transfer, Exchange › Owe, Debt, Cancel
s.d: to release a person from the obligation of repaying what is owed
s.g: to cancel a debt; to forgive a debt

s.d: to hand someone over into the control of another person, without some reasonable cause
s.g: to hand over to; to put into the control of someone

s.d: a marker of a reason, often with the implication of an underlying purpose
a marker of purpose, pointing to the goal of an event or state
s.g: for the purpose of; for the sake of; in order to

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Kindness, Harshness
s.d: to show kindness to someone, with the implication of graciousness on the part of the one showing such kindness
s.g: to show kindness; to manifest graciousness toward; kindness; graciousness; grace
s.c: It is important to note that kindness in English indicates an activity in which an individual is kind to someone; it is essentially an event involving a particular quality. The same is true of χάρις in ⟦Acts 15:40|Acts 15:40⟧, for this is not a mere gracious disposition, but an expectation of the Lord’s showing kindness.

s.d: (derivative of {L:χαρίζομαι<SDBG:χαρίζομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to give graciously and generously,’ {D:57.102}) that which is given freely and generously
s.c: χάρις may also occur in contexts in which the meaning of ‘generous gift’ may imply the purpose of gaining some favor or benefit. In ⟦Acts 24:27|Acts 24:27⟧ (θέλων τε χάριτα καταθέσθαι τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις ὁ Φῆλιξ ‘Felix wanted to be offered a generous gift by the Jews’) the implication is that of ‘a bribe,’ but probably spoken of euphemistically here as ‘a gift.’

s.d: an expression of thankfulness{N:001}

s.dp: Attitudes and Emotions › Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
s.d: a favorable attitude toward someone or something
s.c: In the expressions ἔχοντες χάριν πρὸς ὅλον τὸν λαόν (⟦Acts 2:47|Acts 2:47⟧) and εὗρες γὰρ χάριν παρὰ τῷ θεῷ (⟦Luke 1:30|Luke 1:30⟧) it would appear on the basis of superficial examination that the subject of the participle or the verb is in some respects an active agent. Semantically, however, the subject is actually the recipient of the good will, and in these contexts it is either the people or God who takes pleasure in or is pleased by the grammatical subjects in question. These expressions are typical of situations in which the semantic relationships are almost completely the reverse of the syntactic relationships.

s.d: (derivative of {L:χαρίζομαι<SDBG:χαρίζομαι:000000>}[a] ‘to give graciously and generously,’ {D:57.102}) that which is given freely and generously

s.dp: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior › Kindness, Harshness
s.d: to show kindness to someone, with the implication of graciousness on the part of the one showing such kindness
s.g: to show kindness; to manifest graciousness toward; kindness; graciousness; grace
s.c: It is important to note that kindness in English indicates an activity in which an individual is kind to someone; it is essentially an event involving a particular quality. The same is true of χάρις in ⟦Acts 15:40|Acts 15:40⟧, for this is not a mere gracious disposition, but an expectation of the Lord’s showing kindness.

s.dp: Names of Persons and Places › Places
s.d: a city in Mesopotamia

s.dp: Artifacts › Instruments Used in Marking and Writing
s.d: a sheet of papyrus used for writing

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Depressions and Holes
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of χάσμα ‘yawning,’ not occurring in the NT) a deep, unbridgeable valley or trough between two points
s.c: In this only NT occurrence of χάσμα the reference is to the impassable space between two parts of the supernatural abode of the dead. Translators frequently use a descriptive phrase such as ‘a deep valley which no one may cross’ or ‘a space which cannot be crossed.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Land in Contrast With the Sea
s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of χεῖλος ‘lip,’ not occurring in the NT, except as a metonymy for speech; see χεῖλος[b] {D:33.74}) the strip of land close to a body of water
s.c: In the NT contexts in which παράλιος (LN 1.61), χεῖλος, and αἰγιαλός (LN 1.63) occur, it is possible to say that χεῖλος ‘shore’ probably involves a somewhat narrower strip of land than παράλιος ‘a coastal region,’ but χεῖλος evidently denotes a somewhat wider area than αἰγιαλός ‘beach, shore.’

s.d: (figurative extension of meaning of χεῖλος ‘lip,’ not occurring in the NT) to communicate orally
to be overtaken by or to experience stormy weather
s.g: to undergo bad weather; to be in a storm
s.c: In some languages it may be appropriate to translate χειμάζομαι in an idiomatic form, for example, ‘the wind and rain caught us’ or ‘the storm trapped us.’

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Bodies of Water
s.d: a stream or river which flows only during the rainy season (in Palestine this would be during the winter months) or when melting snow from the mountains provides running water for a relatively short period of time
s.c: The reference in ⟦John 18:1|John 18:1⟧ is probably to the narrow valley, not to the stream itself, as noted in LN 1.52.

s.dp: Geographical Objects and Features › Depressions and Holes
s.d: a ravine or narrow valley in which a stream flows during the rainy season, but which is normally dry during the dry season
s.c: In desert areas of the world designations for such ravines or valleys are common enough; in fact, there may be several different terms to describe different types of wadis, but for tropical areas and for most temperate parts of the world, it may seem incredible that rivers would regularly dry up during part of the year. What is important, however, in the biblical context in which χείμαρρος ‘a seasonal stream,’ LN 1.77).

s.dp: Time › Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
s.d: the coldest season of the year
s.c: In a number of languages it may be important to translate χειμών as simply ‘the time of the cold rains.’ Such rains may actually occur during the growing season or as a part of the rainy season. In semi-tropical areas, however, the cold rains do normally occur in what is regarded as the winter, while the warm rains occur in the summer. See also discussion at LN 67.163.

s.d: stormy weather involving strong wind, overcast sky, and often cold temperature; thunder and lightning may also be present
s.c: The principal difficulty involved in translating χειμών is the fact that in so many languages there are quite distinct terms for various kinds of bad weather or storms. Furthermore, the location of such bad weather will also influence significantly the terms which may be used. For example, stormy weather over the open sea may require quite a different term from what would be used in speaking of a similar kind of storm over the land. In addition, storms which are accompanied by rain may also be referred to by different terms from those which involve wind without rain. Accordingly, one must carefully examine each biblical context in which χειμών is employed and determine what would be the most satisfactory expression in the receptor language. For example, in ⟦Matthew 16:3|Matthew 16:3⟧ the reference is to a windstorm accompanied by clouds and moving over land, while in ⟦Acts 27:20|Acts 27:20⟧ the reference is to a storm of long duration which takes place over a body of water.

s.dp: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products › Parts of the Body
s.d: a hand or any relevant portion of the hand, including, for example, the fingers
s.c: In rendering ⟦Matthew 8:3|Matthew 8:3⟧ it would be inappropriate in some languages to translate literally ‘he stretched out his hand,’ since this would imply some kind of miracle of extending the hand itself. A correct rendering may be ‘he extended his arm and touched him with his hand.’|In ⟦Luke 15:22|Luke 15:22⟧ χείρ refers to the finger, not to the hand, and therefore it is necessary to translate in most languages ‘put a ring on his finger.’

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:χείρ<SDBG:χείρ:000000>}[a] ‘hand,’ {D:8.30}) a human as an agent in some activity{N:001}
(a figurative extension of meaning of {L:χείρ<SDBG:χείρ:000000>}[a] ‘hand,’ {D:8.30}) power as an expression of the activity of a person or supernatural being{N:002}
s.c: In some languages there is no abstract term for ‘power.’ The equivalent of doing something by the power of someone is ‘someone makes it possible to do’ or, in a figurative sense, ‘someone gives strength to do.’

s.d: (a figurative extension of meaning of {L:χείρ<SDBG:χείρ:000000>}[a] ‘hand,’ {D:8.30}) a state of control exercised by a person
s.g: to be in the control of; to be in the power of
s.c: In some languages it may be necessary to express the meaning of ‘control’ in the context of ⟦Acts 12:11|Acts 12:11⟧ by a more specific reference to potential action, for example, ‘he rescued me and Herod could not do anything to me.’

s.d: (an idiom, literally: to give into the hands) to hand someone over into the control of others
s.g: to deliver to the control of; to hand over to
s.c: In a context such as ⟦Matthew 26:45|Matthew 26:45⟧, παραδίδοται εἰς χεῖρας may be rendered as ‘will hand him over to be arrested’ or ‘will cause him to be taken into custody.’

s.dp: Case › Agent, Personal or Nonpersonal, Causative or Immediate, Direct or Indirect
s.d: (an idiom, literally: with the hand of) a marker of an associated agent
(an idiom, literally: human hand) a human being as a means of accomplishing something

s.dp: Control, Rule › Seize, Take into Custody
s.d: (an idiom, literally: to lay hands on) to take a person into custody for alleged illegal activity{N:003}
(a Semitic idiom, literally: one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back) to begin some activity requiring close attention but then to change one’s mind about proceeding
s.g: to start to do something and then to hesitate; to begin but have second thoughts about continuing
s.c: It is probably best to regard the phrase ἐπιβαλὼν τὴν χεῖρα ἐπ᾽ ἄροτρον καὶ βλέπων εἰς τὰ ὀπίσω as a part of a traditional saying referring to anyone who has second thoughts about undertaking some new or different enterprise, but the particular manner in which this is adapted to a statement concerning ‘the kingdom of God’ makes its strictly idiomatic structure somewhat doubtful.

s.dp: Control, Rule › Seize, Take into Custody
s.d: (an idiom, literally to stretch out hands upon) to take a person into custody for alleged illegal activity
to lead or guide by taking by the hand
s.g: to lead someone by the hand; to take by the hand

s.d: (derivative of {L:χειραγωγέω<SDBG:χειραγωγέω:000000>} ‘to lead by the hand,’ {D:15.184}) a person who leads another by the hand
s.g: a guide; one who leads by the hand

s.d: a handwritten statement, especially a record of financial accounts (similar in meaning to {L:γράμμα<SDBG:γράμμα:000003>}[d] ‘account,’ {D:33.39}, but perhaps with emphasis upon the handwritten nature of the document)
pertaining to what has been made by someone
